source.title: Exploring Layer-wise Representations of English and Chinese Homonymy in Pre-trained Language Models
source.authors: M. K. Ma; Chenwei Xie; Wen-Bo Wang; W. S. Wang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures homonym representation scores across model families and sizes, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit or test scaling laws, or evaluate the claim versions. Its size-related results concern a different construct.
record.gate_note: The paper reports D-scores for homonym representations and discusses whether homonym disambiguation consistently improves with model size. These are not loss-scaling, downstream-task-performance, or compute-allocation results. The D-score measurements are recorded as related findings, not as evidence for a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study measures a homonym disambiguation score (D-score) computed from hidden-state angular similarities across 21 pretrained models. It does not measure held-out loss, fit power laws, test compute allocation or extrapolation, or vary architecture at fixed parameter count. The D-score is a representational probe, not downstream task performance, so V6 is not tested either. Section 4.4 cites Kaplan et al. and compares D-score across sizes within families. That is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version. The models also differ in training data and recipe within families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B vs 3.2), so size is not cleanly isolated.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors report three findings: no universal best layer for homonym disambiguation; bidirectional and multilingual models outperform much larger autoregressive models; and models separate different-POS homonyms better than same-POS ones, opposite to human findings. Size does not consistently help, but this is a secondary point (Sec 4.4). Their main conclusion is that individual model differences call for controlled interpretability experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses contextualized word representations and an angular-similarity-based D-score to analyze homonym disambiguation; it does not use a scaling-law loss-fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported D-score varies with model family, language, and layer; English D-scores are reported as significantly higher than Chinese scores across included models.

fits_no_version.finding: Best-layer homonym D-score does not rise consistently with parameter count within families (Table 1, Sec 4.4). English results: BERT and GPT-2 larger models score higher; Llama 3B is about equal to 8B (16.86 vs 16.87); Qwen 1.5B is highest (15.11 vs 13.99 for 7B). Chinese results: gpt2 beats gpt2-medium. Differences within GPT-2 and Qwen are non-significant. DeBERTa-v3-large (434M) exceeds 7-8B autoregressive models on English.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contextual homonym disambiguation in hidden representations does not scale monotonically with model size; architecture and multilingual pretraining data matter more.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2025)
record.problems: The study uses LLM-generated sentences, which the authors note may be biased or unnatural; English homonyms are restricted to base forms; and the study lacks direct human-related data for comparison. These limitations concern its homonym-representation findings, not scaling-law loss evidence.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Effect of depth/width at fixed parameter count on loss.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream task performance versus scale or loss. The D-score is a representation-geometry probe, not a task metric.
Dependence of fitted exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup choices.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The state cannot_determine is acceptable since no version is measured. Sizes match Table 1. The 'operation: scaling' label is loose: models within a family differ in data and training recipe, not just size. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating loss from small runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Architecture changes at fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss; the paper measures homonym representation D-scores instead.
Dependence of fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices.
